$comment: Who says which words in this chapter (docs/voice-narration-plan.md section 3). Drafted by `npm run voice:script`; a line with no entry is read by the narrator. A person checks each draft and sets `reviewed` to true; re-drafting only touches missing and stale entries.

lines.text: A grandmother with glasses on a chain drops her pencil.
"Well! Look who came home the FRONT way."
Four aunts hug you. Then her face goes serious.
"Worst season in the tallies, love. Come and help."
At the gate, a dragonling grandmother passes a bell over each pack and tallies every ring.
"No digging tools past the stones. Your turn."
She adjusts her glasses, then her pencil, then her glasses again.
Rope, socks, a squashed sandwich, a spoon. Not one pick, not one shovel, and you never once say the word treasure. The grandmother taps her pencil on her teeth. "Not diggers," she writes.
"Very tidy."
She waves you through with a look that is almost respect.
The grandmother checks what you carry and tallies anything that hums.
"The tally house will want your story."
She sends you through, after checking your socks twice.
You hold up the witch's charm. It rings with the grandmother's bell, the very same note.
"That's Thrum's work!"
she says.
"Is that old crow still at the ford? Anybody Thrum trusts can skip my socks."
In the gate town, bells hang from poles, from packs and from one goat.
"Take what the mountain drops,"
says a grandmother.
"Never pry at what it holds."
A man with a huge pry bar says he did not hear. The goat heard.
You plant your feet and say it exactly like your grandmother, finger wagging:
"Take what the mountain drops. Never pry at what it holds. And wipe your feet."
Every grandmother nods so hard her glasses bounce.
He watches the whole thing, nods along, says
"Right, right,"
and marches off up the hill with his pry bar anyway. You follow him, because somebody should.
The prospector gives up his pry bar. A grandmother hangs it on a wall of hundreds.
"Every one of those listened, in the end."
She finds a hook between two very stubborn ones.
Out past the stones, the grandmothers fish you out of the heather, one collar at a time. They bandage your scrapes.
"Bandages cost, this season,"
says one, over her glasses. Up the hill, the crabs clack, very pleased with themselves.
Wend thinks for a long time.
"Everything that hums wants to go home,"
Wend says at last.
"We'd like to help it get there, all at once."
It sounds lovely. It also sounds like something nobody should do on a guess. You go up to the tally house thinking about it.
"We said no,"
you tell Wend,
"on the north road."
Wend nods.
"I remember."
Wend fills your bowls anyway, just as warmly.
"Soup's still free. Kindness first."
The crystal hums the same note as your packs.
Wend hugs everybody and shows the tent your names in the little book.
"These ones helped,"
Wend says, and everybody claps. It is very warm in the tent. You are not sure you like it.
In the tally house, Great-Grandma Ashby, the oldest grandmother of all, opens a big book full of tidy eruption marks. This season's page is mostly question marks.
"Show me what you know,"
she says, tapping her walking stick.
"We will compare."
The witch's charm rings the moment you hold it up. Ashby goes very still. She opens the oldest book and points to a mark like a little bell.
"Same note. My great-great-grandma heard it too."
Ashby puts chalk in your hand and taps the clues on the floor map, one at a time.
"Watch,"
she says.
"Then put them back the same way. Slowly, dears."
"One more thing,"
says Ashby.
"The boundary stones were here first. Before the first families. Already marking the line we mark now."
Everything you have seen points one way: the stones are older than the mountain's name, and the land has always kept count.

On the oldest stone, under the moss, are rows of marks worn almost smooth. They are tally marks, like the grandmothers' marks, but far older. Somebody was counting here before the first families came. The land has been keeping records. Great-Grandma Ashby only nods.
"Now come and see my shelf."
The marks are worn so smooth you cannot tell scratches from weather. Great-Grandma Ashby takes your hand and runs your fingers along them: one, one, one, and a gap.
"Counting,"
she says.
"Before us. Come and see the shelf."
On a shelf behind Ashby, something glints. She sees you looking.
"Clever eyes,"
she says. She reaches up with her stick, as gently as you would touch a sleeping baby's blanket.
"Come here, then. Carefully."
A fresh-fallen gem rests on an old list of caves nobody may gather in.
"Keeping,"
says Ashby.
"Not hiding."
Her stick straightens the list without touching the gem. You could ask to carry it north, as proof.
You leave the stone on its list. Ashby squares the paper with her stick.
"Some things want keeping more than carrying."
The shelf hums softly behind you.
You hold a warm rock in both hands and ask the proper way, the way every dragonling child learns. Ashby presses her lips tight. Then she sets the gem on top of your rock.
"Keeping. Not taking. Don't you dare sell it."
Two hands, slow as a snail, and you square the list after with one finger. Great-Grandma Ashby wraps the gem in a page torn from nothing important and puts it in your hands.
"The Unassigned Stone. Keep it. Don't you dare sell it."
Your fingers bump the list crooked, and you grab at the gem as if it might run off. Great-Grandma Ashby pats your hand.
"You'll know the difference soon. Not today."
The stone stays on its list, and somehow that feels right too.
Embermoths stream south over the porch. A bell rings once. The town's bell-code expert, a dragonling of about six, tugs your sleeve.
"One ring. Moths leaving,"
she says.
"Every night this month."

An embermoth lands in your hands, warm as cocoa. Then it notices your pack. It lifts off and loops wide around the humming thing inside, then flies south with the others. The small dragonling pats your arm.
"They all do that."
"They always leave a little before the mountain wakes,"
says the small dragonling, very fast,
"and come back after. Grandmothers count everything."
She frowns.
"But never this many. And they haven't come back."
Supper in the bell house is a long table, forty grandmothers, and bread baked on hot rocks. Ashby taps the table.
"Old rule. Every guest brings something: a story, a recipe, a thing from the road."
Forty pairs of glasses turn your way.
You set the Depot Stone on the table. The bell house goes silent. Ashby holds up its SOLD tag with two fingers, as if it smells.
"Nobody sells what the mountain drops."
She drops the tag in the fire.
"Now you're keeping it. Not owning it."
The bell-code expert shakes you awake. Three lanterns bob up toward a hillside cave.
"That cave's on the list,"
she whispers.
"Nobody gathers there."
Her slippers are on the wrong feet.
Eleven grandmothers march uphill in nightgowns, ringing hand bells. The lanterns wobble, then flee downhill. Ashby comes back yawning.
"Thank you, dears. Back to bed."
At dawn, the bell-code expert has jobs.
"Learn the big-bell crew's passing line,"
she says, very fast,
"or polish hand bells for a chorus. Both help at the stones, if you get them right!"
The bell in the corner hangs untouched, its rope tied high.
The small dragonling, who has talked nonstop since yesterday, stops.
"Nobody rings that one,"
she says quietly.
"Not ever. Great-Grandma says we'll know."
She touches its rim on tiptoe. It is cold, in a house of warm stones.
With the crowd calm, a centaur guide named Perrin Nine-Verse beckons you behind a stone.
"There's a Shortcut through the hills,"
he whispers.
"My family has argued about it for nine generations. Will you walk it?"
The Shortcut is real. It runs through a crack in a hill and comes out at the last boundary stone, a whole day ahead. Perrin has tears in his eyes.
"Never tell anyone,"
he says.
"It's the best argument we've got."
You choose the caravan road. Perrin is so relieved he has to sit down.
"Good! The argument lives,"
he says.
"My grandfather would be furious if it ended on a Tuesday."
He gallops off to argue with someone.
Perrin reads Old Corran's bark, lips moving. Then he goes pale.
"Corran's new verses bend around the Shortcut too. It's been in the song all along."
He hands it back with shaking hooves.
"Don't tell Corran."
At the last stone, Sergeant Holloway from the north road has a ledger open.
"You again. Good. I need counters. Picks going north: four hundred and twelve. Picks back: nine. I dislike this arithmetic."
You count, and count, and your number matches the sergeant's exactly. Holloway writes your names in the ledger under 'Counters, Reliable,' which is apparently a great honor.
"The citadel keeps logs,"
the sergeant says.
"Somebody has to."
You count four hundred and twelve picks, two goats and a very tall hat. Holloway checks your sums, crosses out the goats, keeps the hat, and writes you down as 'Counters, Enthusiastic.'
"Close enough,"
says the sergeant.
"For arithmetic."
"We write it down,"
says Holloway.
"Every pick, every ash wind, every moth night. It all goes up to Redspire and onto a shelf."
The sergeant closes the ledger.
"Mostly, nobody reads it."
Your griffin and the sergeant swap sky news: ash over the peak every evening, moths flying south, warm wind where it should be cold. Holloway writes it all down.
"Same as our logs,"
the sergeant says quietly.
Ashby meets you at the stone.
"Who hears what you found first?"
she asks.
"The Skywardens keep logs at their citadel. We grandmothers can ring it through the bell towns. Or you can keep it close."
She taps her stick and waits.
A relay runner carries your story to the Skywardens. Ashby sniffs.
"They do write things down."
She checks that the runner's cord is tied properly.
You keep what you found to yourselves. Ashby nods.
"Careful is not the same as quiet. But careful is a start."
The bells ring their ordinary morning rings.
You and the prospectors carry their pry bars to the grandmothers' wall, where every tool given up at the stones is hung. A grandmother counts three coins into your hands.
"Wall-hanging rate. Honest work, honestly paid."
The grandmothers wheel their loudest hand bell down to the stones on a little cart. A wheel sticks in a rut.
"Push on the count!"
calls the bell-code expert.
"One, two, NOW!"

On the porch, the hum in your packs jumps. Bone crawlers scuttle out from under the boards, small, pale and many-legged. They love a hum, and they are heading for the tally house books, the best nest a crawler ever saw.
"Not in my books!"
says Ashby.
"Shoo them, dears."
The crawlers scuttle away under the porch in one tidy line. Ashby counts her books twice. Then she hands you a little brass whistle.
"One loud note. Crawlers hate it. So do I."
The first stars are coming out.

You put a coin on the table. A grandmother carries in a pot of honey the size of her head. It goes on bread, on porridge, and once, by mistake, on a glasses case. She slides a honeycake into your pack.
"For the road."
You help Ashby wrap the bells in soft cloths. One gives a tiny ting, and the grandmothers answer with a soft shhh. A grandmother tucks leftover bread into your pack.
"Breakfast,"
she whispers.
He nods along, says
"Right, right,"
and marches up the hill with his pry bar anyway. You follow him, because somebody should.
Your fingers bump the list crooked. Ashby pats your hand.
"You'll know the difference soon. Not today."
The stone stays on its list.
At the stones, the morning crowd is pushing. A man in a feathered hat shouts from a cart that they are only rocks.
"Not one step back, dears,"
say the grandmothers. Help make room, share what you know, or use your bell job.
